title: Lord Byron kept a bear at Cambridge because students weren't allowed dogs

cover.alt: Lord Byron, a young man in a blue tailcoat, holds the chain of a tame brown bear in front of a college gateway.

body: Trinity College, Cambridge, had long banned undergraduates from keeping dogs in college. In the autumn of 1807 the 19-year-old **Lord Byron** came back with a tame bear instead. 'When I brought him here,' he wrote to his friend Elizabeth Pigot on 26 October, 'they asked me what I meant to do with him, and my reply was, "he should sit for a fellowship." … This answer delighted them not.' The bear probably lived in a stable in the town rather than in college, and Byron left Cambridge for good within a few months. In 1809 he joked in print that jealous rivals had kept the bear from its fellowship. By 1811 the bear was dead.

slides.alt: A college court of pale stone with a gateway. Young Lord Byron stands beside his big black dog while a stern don in a black gown and mortarboard points at it.
slides.caption: Trinity College, Cambridge, 1807. The rules are clear: no dogs in college.

bubbles.text: No dogs, my lord. Statutes are statutes.

slides.alt: Byron, grinning, leads a big brown bear on a chain through the college gateway. The don stares, appalled.
slides.caption: Autumn term, 1807. Byron, 19, comes back with a tame bear.

bubbles.text: And what do you mean to do with him?
bubbles.speaker: A college fellow

slides.alt: In a panelled college room the bear sits up wearing a mortarboard, between a smirking Byron and a grim don.
slides.caption: His answer 'delighted them not', Byron told a friend. Later he claimed jealous rivals had blocked the bear's fellowship.

slides.question: What did Byron say his bear would do at Trinity?
options: Win a bet with the Master
slides.explanation: 'He should sit for a fellowship,' he told the college, as he reported in a letter of 26 October 1807. 'This answer delighted them not.'
